claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are sparsely active, spontaneously and during sensory stimulation.
source: Layer (L) 2/3 pyramidal neurons in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are sparsely active, spontaneously and during sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section (Barth and Poulet, 2012; O'Connor et al., 2010).

claim: POm more robustly depolarized L2/3 cells compared to M1 and S2 inputs.
source: POm, however, more robustly depolarized L2/3 cells and, when paired with peripheral stimulation, evoked action potentials.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 4, showing larger PSP amplitudes for POm compared to M1 and S2.

claim: POm, when paired with peripheral stimulation, evoked action potentials in L2/3 cells.
source: POm, however, more robustly depolarized L2/3 cells and, when paired with peripheral stimulation, evoked action potentials.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D showing increased spiking responses when POm activation is combined with whisker stimulation.

claim: POm triggered a stronger fast-onset depolarization than M1 and S2.
source: POm triggered not only a stronger fast-onset depolarization but also a delayed all-or-none persistent depolarization, lasting up to 1 s and exhibiting alpha/beta-range oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2 and 4 showing larger initial PSP amplitudes for POm.

claim: POm triggered a delayed all-or-none persistent depolarization lasting up to 1 s.
source: POm triggered not only a stronger fast-onset depolarization but also a delayed all-or-none persistent depolarization, lasting up to 1 s and exhibiting alpha/beta-range oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing prolonged depolarization following POm activation.

claim: POm-triggered persistent depolarization exhibits alpha/beta-range oscillations.
source: POm triggered not only a stronger fast-onset depolarization but also a delayed all-or-none persistent depolarization, lasting up to 1 s and exhibiting alpha/beta-range oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 5C demonstrating 10-20 Hz oscillations during persistent depolarization.

claim: Inactivating POm somata abolished persistent but not initial depolarization.
source: Inactivating POm somata abolished persistent but not initial depolarization, indicating a recurrent circuit mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological inactivation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The persistent depolarization is generated through a recurrent circuit mechanism involving POm.
source: Inactivating POm somata abolished persistent but not initial depolarization, indicating a recurrent circuit mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological inactivation data in Figure 8, which shows that POm somatic activity is necessary for persistent depolarization.

claim: Secondary thalamus can enhance L2/3 responsiveness over long periods.
source: We conclude that secondary thalamus can enhance L2/3 responsiveness over long periods.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental findings of persistent depolarization lasting up to 1 second.

claim: The timescales of POm-induced depolarization could provide a potential modality-specific substrate for attention, working memory, and plasticity.
source: Such timescales could provide a potential modality-specific substrate for attention, working memory, and plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed timescales of persistent depolarization and comparison to known functions of secondary thalamus.

claim: L2/3 firing probability remains low in awake animals performing simple tactile detection tasks.
source: Even in awake animals performing simple tactile detection tasks, L2/3 firing probability remains low (O'Connor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor et al., 2010.

claim: Sensory inputs during active whisking reliably evoke short-latency subthreshold depolarization in L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In the whisker representation (barrel cortex) of rodent primary somatosensory cortex (S1), sensory inputs during active whisking reliably evoke short-latency subthreshold depolarization in L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Crochet et al., 2011; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crochet et al., 2011 and Sachidhanandam et al., 2013.

claim: Sensory input engages strong feed-forward inhibition, which keeps membrane potential of most L2/3 neurons below spike threshold.
source: Sensory input also engages strong feed-forward inhibition, which keeps membrane potential (Vm) of most L2/3 neurons below spike threshold, rendering them quiet or only sparsely responsive (Crochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crochet et al., 2011.

claim: Presenting complex spatio-temporal patterns of whisker stimulation optimized for individual neurons strongly engages neurons in L4-6, but not L2/3.
source: We recently showed that presenting complex spatio-temporal patterns of whisker stimulation optimized for individual neurons strongly engages neurons in L4-6, but not L2/3 (Ramirez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramirez et al., 2014.

claim: Ascending sensory information arriving in L2/3 from L4 alone may be insufficient to drive L2/3 activity.
source: These previous studies suggest that ascending sensory information arriving in L2/3 from L4 alone may be insufficient to drive L2/3 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing sparse L2/3 activity despite sensory stimulation.

claim: L2/3 neurons in S1 receive inputs from M1.
source: L2/3 neurons in S1 receive inputs from higher-order cortical and subcortical regions, such as the primary motor cortex (M1) (Kinnischtzke et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Petreanu et al., 2009; Veinante and Deschênes, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Kinnischtzke et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Petreanu et al., 2009; Veinante and Deschênes, 2003).

claim: L2/3 neurons in S1 receive inputs from POm.
source: and the secondary somatosensory nucleus of the thalamus, called the posterior medial (POm) nucleus (Jouhanneau et al., 2014; Lu and Lin, 1993; Ohno et al., 2012; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Sherman and Guillery, 2011; Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Jouhanneau et al., 2014; Lu and Lin, 1993; Ohno et al., 2012; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Sherman and Guillery, 2011; Wimmer et al., 2010).

claim: POm is a potent driver of activity in secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) in vitro.
source: POm is known to be a potent driver of activity in secondary somatosensory (S2) in vitro (Theyel et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Theyel et al., 2010.

claim: POm input can enhance the responsiveness of L5 pyramidal neurons to sensory stimulation in vivo in anesthetized mice.
source: and a recent in vivo study of anesthetized mice found that POm input could enhance the responsiveness of L5 pyramidal neurons to sensory stimulation (Mease et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mease et al., 2016.

claim: S1 receives significant anatomical input from S2.
source: Additionally S1 receives significant anatomical input from S2 (Cauller et al., 1998), whose effects remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cauller et al., 1998.

claim: POm axons were concentrated in L4 septum and L5A.
source: Outside of L1, axonal distributions across varied based on the area of origin (Figure 1A, top): POm axons were concentrated in L4 septum and L5A
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: M1 axons resided mostly in deep L5B and L6.
source: M1 axons resided mostly in deep L5B and L6
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: S2 axons formed bands in both L5 and L6.
source: and S2 axons formed bands in both L5 and L6 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Axons from POm, M1, and S2 all avoided L4 barrels.
source: Axons from all three regions avoided L4 barrels and were rare in L3.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Axons from POm, M1, and S2 were rare in L3.
source: Axons from all three regions avoided L4 barrels and were rare in L3.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No labeled somata were observed in barrel cortex after viral infection of POm, M1, or S2.
source: No labeled somata were ever observed in barrel cortex, even after immunohistochemical amplification, ruling out retrograde infection of S1 neurons.
evidence: This is based on histological observations and rules out a potential confound.

claim: Photo-activation of POm axons elicited EPSPs in 21 out of 33 L2/3 neurons.
source: Photo-activation of POm axons elicited EPSPs in the majority of recorded neurons (21 out of 33 neurons; Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: POm-evoked EPSPs had a mean amplitude of 4.2 ± 0.8 mV in responsive neurons.
source: which were substantial in size (mean ± SEM, 4.2 ± 0.8 mV).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: M1 inputs produced EPSPs in 5 out of 19 L2/3 neurons with mean amplitude of 1.2 ± 0.48 mV.
source: By comparison, M1 and S2 inputs produced significantly smaller responses in L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2C) (M1: 5 out of 19 neurons, 1.2 ± 0.48 mV
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: S2 inputs produced EPSPs in 15 out of 22 L2/3 neurons with mean amplitude of 1.3 ± 0.28 mV.
source: S2: 15 out of 22 neurons, 1.3 ± 0.28 mV
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: POm-evoked responses were significantly larger than M1 and S2 responses (one-way ANOVA, p < 10-5).
source: one-way ANOVA, p < 10-5= 0.006
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the experimental data.

claim: When analyzing all neurons including non-responders, POm responses (2.7 ± 0.6 mV) were significantly larger than M1 (0.16 ± 0.22 mV) and S2 (0.87 ± 0.23 mV) responses (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.0015).
source: Photo-activation of POm axons was also significantly larger when the full population of neurons, with and without EPSPs, were analyzed (POm: n = 33, mean ± SEM 2.7 ± 0.6 mV; M1: n = 19, mean 0.16 mV ± 0.22 mV; S2: n = 22, mean 0.87 ± 0.23 mV; one-way ANOVA, p = 0.0015; Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the experimental data including all recorded neurons.

claim: Baseline membrane potential did not differ among POm, M1, and S2 groups (one-way ANOVA, p=0.92).
source: Neurons recorded in POm-infected animals had baseline membrane potential (Vm; Figure 2E) and input resistance (Rin; Figure 2F) similar to those in M1- and S2-infected animals
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Input resistance did not differ among POm, M1, and S2 groups (one-way ANOVA, p=0.85).
source: Neurons recorded in POm-infected animals had baseline membrane potential (Vm; Figure 2E) and input resistance (Rin; Figure 2F) similar to those in M1- and S2-infected animals
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The kinetics of photo-activated EPSPs (onset latencies, rise times, and decay times) were similar across M1, S2, and POm experiments.
source: Additionally, the kinetics of photo-activated EPSPs (onset latencies, rise times, and decay times) were similar across M1, S2, and POm experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Virus occasionally spread along the injection pipette track into high-order visual thalamic nuclei LP and LD, superficial to POm.
source: Virus occasionally spread along the injection pipette track and into high-order visual thalamic nuclei LP and LD, superficial to POm (Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis.

claim: LP and LD thalamic nuclei do not target barrel cortex.
source: These two nuclei, however, do not target barrel cortex (Kamishina et al., 2009; van Groen and Wyss, 1992) and are unlikely to explain our observations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kamishina et al., 2009 and van Groen and Wyss, 1992.

claim: L2/3 cells with the strongest POm inputs could be observed in the same animals having cells receiving relatively weak POm input—up to 10 times smaller.
source: Moreover, for animals in which multiple cortical neurons were patched, L2/3 cells with the strongest POm inputs could be observed in the same animals having cells receiving relatively weak POm input—up to 10 times smaller (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strongest POm inputs are unlikely to result solely from variability in injection placement or viral efficiency.
source: This indicates that the strongest POm inputs are unlikely to result solely from variability in injection placement or viral efficiency and, conceivably, may reflect L2/3 cell variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that strong and weak POm inputs occur in the same animals.

claim: Photo-activation of long-range axons from POm, M1, or S2 rarely suppressed sensory responses.
source: Comparison of the combined stimuli and whisker stimulus alone showed that photo-activation of long-range axons from any of the three regions rarely suppressed sensory responses if at all (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Only POm projections facilitated L2/3 neuron input when combined with sensory stimulation.
source: Only POm projections (Figure 3B, red) ever facilitated L2/3 neuron input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: Combined light and sensory stimuli elicited sub-threshold responses that were similar to the linear sum of responses to each individual stimulus in most cells.
source: In most cells, combined light and sensory stimuli elicited sub-threshold responses that were similar to the linear sum of the cell's responses to each individual stimulus, suggesting that sensory input and each of these long-range inputs are linearly integrated passively by the L2/3 neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C showing linear summation.

claim: Cells receiving the strongest POm inputs often exhibited sublinear integration.
source: An exception is the group of cells receiving the strongest POm inputs, which often exhibited sublinear integration (filled symbols) as expected from basic cellular properties (i.e., reduced driving force).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C and is explained by known cellular biophysics.

claim: L2/3 neurons in anesthetized animals lacked clear spiking responses to whisker stimuli.
source: L2/3 neurons in anesthetized animals lacked clear spiking responses to whisker stimuli as observed previously (Brecht et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brecht et al., 2003.

claim: Only photo-activation of POm axons significantly facilitates sensory responses of L2/3 pyramidal neurons (paired t-test: POm, n = 16, p=0.027).
source: Only photo-activation of POm axons significantly facilitates sensory responses of L2/3 pyramidal neurons (paired t-test: POm, n = 16, p=0.027; M1, n = 5, p=0.86; S2, n = 13, p=0.95).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: POm neurons fire at lower rates under anesthesia than during wakefulness.
source: Under anesthesia, POm neurons fire at lower rates than during wakefulness (Masri et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2008.

claim: Cortical dynamics, intracellular membrane potential, and sensory responses recorded in the fentanyl sedation preparation resemble those recorded in awake animals.
source: Previous studies have shown that cortical dynamics, intracellular membrane potential, and sensory responses recorded in this sedated preparation resemble those recorded in awake animals (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Simons et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Constantinople and Bruno, 2011 and Simons et al., 1992.

claim: POm axons induced larger EPSPs in sedated animals (5.5 ± 1.0 mV) than in urethane-anesthetized animals (p=0.004).
source: POm axons continued to induce substantial EPSPs in sedated animals, even larger than that found in urethane-anesthetized animals (Figure 4A, red).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: M1 axons were significantly more effective under sedation (3.1 ± 1.4 mV) than under urethane anesthesia (p=0.009).
source: M1 axons were also significantly more effective under sedation (yellow), but did not reach the same potency as POm inputs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: S2 inputs were similarly weak under both sedation and urethane anesthesia conditions (p=0.13).
source: S2 inputs were similarly weak under both conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Regression of initial POm input magnitude against baseline membrane potential predicts a reversal potential of −34 mV.
source: Despite the larger magnitude of POm input, the pathway appears to be engaging significant inhibition: Regression of initial POm input magnitude against baseline membrane potential predicts a reversal potential of −34 mV, suggestive of mixed excitation and inhibition and consistent with other inputs to L2/3 pyramids in vivo (Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of experimental data and is consistent with cited literature (Petersen et al., 2003).

claim: POm input appeared overall more potent relative to S2 and M1 inputs under both light sedation and general anesthesia.
source: In summary, POm input appeared overall more potent relative to S2 and M1 inputs under very different states—both light sedation and general anesthesia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from both anesthetized and sedated conditions.

claim: POm infections were an order of magnitude larger in cross-sectional area than any potential VPM contamination.
source: POm infections were an order of magnitude larger in cross-sectional area than any potential VPM contamination.
evidence: This is based on histological measurements of infection size.

claim: PSP amplitude correlated with the size of the infected region in POm (p = 0.016), not VPM (p = 0.63).
source: PSP amplitude correlated with the size of the infected region in POm, not the one in VPM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no statistically significant relationship between POm input magnitude and recording depth from the pia (p=0.18).
source: Additionally, we observed no statistically significant relationship of POm input magnitude and recording depth from the pia (regression, p=0.18), indicating that L2 and L3 pyramids were similarly affected by photo-activation
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: L2 and L3 pyramids were similarly affected by POm photo-activation.
source: indicating that L2 and L3 pyramids were similarly affected by photo-activation even though L3 pyramids are more likely than L2 pyramids to receive VPM input.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of relationship between recording depth and POm input magnitude.

claim: There was no relationship between the horizontal distance of L2/3 somata from the center of the nearest barrel column and the magnitude of POm input (R2 = 0.06, p=0.4).
source: There was, however, no relationship of distance to the magnitude of POm input (Figure 4B; R2 = 0.06, p=0.4), suggesting that septal innervation is not a major contributor to POm's relative potency.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All individual POm axons reconstructed to date branch extensively in L1 but have few or no branches in the septum.
source: This result is consistent with anatomy: all individual POm axons reconstructed to date branch extensively in L1 but have few or no branches in the septum that they traverse to reach L1 (Deschênes et al., 1998; Ohno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschênes et al., 1998 and Ohno et al., 2012.

claim: A single POm axon often ascends the septal spaces between more than one pair of barrels.
source: Additionally, a single POm axon often ascends the septal spaces between more than one pair of barrels.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the literature.

claim: S2 and M1 axon stimulation did not significantly enhance L2/3 neurons' responses to whisker stimulation under sedation.
source: We did not detect any statistically significant enhancement of L2/3 neurons' responses to whisker stimulation by S2 or M1 axon stimulation (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Photo-activation of POm inputs appeared to slightly boost the sub-threshold responses of L2/3 pyramidal neurons to PW stimulation under sedation, but reached only trend-level significance.
source: Photo-activation of POm inputs appeared to slightly boost the sub-threshold responses of L2/3 pyramidal neurons to PW stimulation under sedation (Figure 4C) as under general anesthesia, but reached only trend-level significance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: POm photo-activation substantially increased suprathreshold (spiking) responses of L2/3 neurons to sensory stimuli.
source: However, this slight subthreshold increase translated into substantial increases of suprathreshold (spiking) responses of those L2/3 neurons to sensory stimuli (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Spiking responses were increased six fold by POm activation (whisker alone: 0.16 ± 0.09 Hz; whisker + light: 1.1 ± 0.36 Hz).
source: Spiking responses were increased six fold (mean ±SEM, whisker stimulus alone: 0.16 ± 0.09 Hz; whisker +light: 1.1 ± 0.36 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: In sedated animals, persistent depolarization in L2/3 pyramidal cells began ~150 ms after POm axon activation (mean onset, 163 ± 13 ms).
source: After the initial fast-onset EPSP and a period of pronounced inhibition, persistent depolarization began ~150 ms after POm axon activation (mean onset, 163 ± 13 ms)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Persistent depolarization typically continued for up to one second (mean duration, 758 ± 133 ms).
source: and typically continued for up to one second (mean duration, 758 ± 133 ms; Figure 5B, red).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For each neuron recorded, ~80% of trials showed a prolonged response to POm activation.
source: For each neuron recorded, ~80% of trials showed a prolonged response, which was unseen in anesthetized animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: M1 and S2 inputs did not elicit persistent depolarization.
source: M1 and S2 inputs did not elicit persistent depolarization (yellow and blue).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VPM axons elicited little or no persistent depolarization in L2/3.
source: Strikingly, axons from VPM elicited little or no persistent depolarization in L2/3 (green), despite generating large initial responses (13.4 ± 3.2 mV; n = 9) that were on average 7-fold larger than those elicited by POm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VPM axons generated large initial responses (13.4 ± 3.2 mV; n = 9) that were on average 7-fold larger than those elicited by POm.
source: despite generating large initial responses (13.4 ± 3.2 mV; n = 9) that were on average 7-fold larger than those elicited by POm.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Persistent depolarization of cortex appears to be a unique capability of secondary thalamus.
source: Thus, persistent depolarization of cortex appears to be a unique capability of secondary thalamus, rather than being a consequence of the magnitude of input generated by a pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of POm and VPM effects.

claim: The persistent depolarization showed clear periodicity in the 10–20 Hz frequency band on individual trials.
source: On individual trials, the persistent depolarization showed clear periodicity in the 10–20 Hz frequency band (Figure 5A,C, red).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and spectral analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: Signals in the 10–20 Hz range were absent from corresponding times during VPM, M1 and S2 axonal photo-activation as well as spontaneous activity.
source: Signals in the 10–20 Hz range were absent from corresponding times during VPM, M1 and S2 axonal photo-activation (green, yellow and blue) as well as spontaneous activity (black).
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Alpha (8–15 Hz) and beta range (12.5–30 Hz) oscillations in cortex appeared to be unique to stimulation of POm axons.
source: Thus, 'alpha' (8–15 Hz) and 'beta' range (12.5–30 Hz) oscillations in cortex appeared to be unique to stimulation of POm axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the spectral analysis comparing POm to other inputs.

claim: The persistent depolarization is detectable in L2/3 local field potentials (LFPs) with inverted polarity relative to whole-cell recordings.
source: The persistent depolarization is also detectable in L2/3 recordings of local field potentials (LFPs), which have inverted polarity relative to whole-cell recordings (compare Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The persistent depolarization elicited by POm axons appeared at all light intensities that evoked an initial response.
source: Varying light intensity over 0.1–35 mW, we found that the persistent depolarization elicited by POm axons appeared at all intensities that evoked an initial response (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The initial peak scaled with light intensity.
source: Whereas the initial peak scaled with light intensity (Figure 6E, top)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The persistent depolarization was virtually all-or-none, appearing with as little as 0.6 mW.
source: the persistent depolarization was virtually all-or-none (middle), appearing with as little as 0.6 mW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: LFP responses to POm in awake rats showed the same characteristic initial and persistent depolarization seen in sedated animals.
source: LFP responses to POm in awake rats showed the same characteristic initial and persistent depolarization (Figure 6C) seen in sedated animals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: During wakefulness POm is able to open an unusually long window of L2/3 depolarization.
source: We conclude that during wakefulness POm is able to open an unusually long window of L2/3 depolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from awake animals.

claim: Spontaneous discharges of POm neurons decreased more than ten-fold when anesthesia was induced (sedated: 13.2 ± 8.7 Hz; anesthetized: 1 ± 1.3 Hz; paired t-test, p=8 × 10−4).
source: Spontaneous discharges of the POm neurons decreased more than ten-fold when anesthesia was induced (sedated mean ±SEM, 13.2 ± 8.7 Hz; anesthetized mean ±SEM, 1 ± 1.3 Hz; paired t-test, p=8 × 10−4; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The POm activity observed during isoflurane-induced anesthesia is similar to that for urethane-anesthetized rats.
source: The activity observed here during isoflurane-induced anesthesia is similar to that for urethane-anesthetized rats (Masri et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2008.

claim: Antidromic POm spiking responses to photostimulation were slightly but not significantly higher under sedation (paired t-test, p=0.09).
source: Antidromic POm spiking responses to photostimulation were slightly but not significantly higher under sedation (paired t-test, p=0.09; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: POm synapses facilitate.
source: Given that POm synapses facilitate (Viaene et al., 2011b), suppressed POm spiking during anesthesia readily explains the smaller fast-onset PSPs compared to sedation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Viaene et al., 2011b.

claim: Five out of nine POm neurons exhibited persistent spiking responses to brief light activation that was statistically (p<0.01) greater than spontaneous activity.
source: Consistent with POm generating the persistent depolarization in L2/3, five out of nine POm neurons exhibited persistent spiking responses to brief light activation of their terminals that was statistically (p<0.01) greater than spontaneous activity (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The initial response in L2/3 remained intact and may have even grown during POm inactivation.
source: We found that the initial response in L2/3 remained intact and may have even grown during inactivation (Figure 8B,C), perhaps due to relief from POm-driven cortical inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: The delayed persistent depolarization was abolished upon POm inactivation.
source: The delayed persistent depolarization, however, was abolished upon inactivation (Figure 8B,D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and 8D.

claim: The delayed persistent depolarization in L2/3 is generated through recurrent circuitry involving POm, rather than a synaptic mechanism or a purely intracortical mechanism.
source: Moreover, this result demonstrates that the delayed persistent depolarization in L2/3 is generated through recurrent circuitry involving POm, rather than a synaptic mechanism or a purely intracortical mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the POm inactivation experiments.

claim: M1 and S2 inputs were relatively weak, having little impact on L2/3 pyramids.
source: In spite of this, M1 and S2 inputs were relatively weak, having little impact on L2/3 pyramids.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data comparing the three pathways.

claim: Only POm inputs appeared sufficient to drive L2/3 neurons and boost their sensory responses.
source: Only POm inputs appeared sufficient to drive L2/3 neurons and boost their sensory responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: The overall laminar distributions of POm, M1, and S2 projections to barrel cortex are consistent with previous studies of the individual projections.
source: The overall laminar distributions of POm, M1, and S2 projections to barrel cortex here are consistent with previous studies of the individual projections (Kinnischtzke et al., 2014; Minamisawa et al., 2018; Ohno et al., 2012; Veinante and Deschênes, 2003; Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: POm, S2 and M1 axons together cover the infragranular layers, from their most shallow depth in L5A to their deepest in L6B.
source: POm, S2 and M1 axons together cover the infragranular layers, from their most shallow depth in L5A to their deepest in L6B.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations from the study.

claim: The S2 zone appears to correspond to the region of L5/6 that lacks POm and VPM innervation.
source: Of note, the S2 zone appears to correspond to the region of L5/6 that lacks POm and VPM innervation (Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited literature (Wimmer et al., 2010).

claim: Within L5 and 6, there potentially exist multiple sub-layers that receive and integrate information from different cortical and subcortical regions.
source: These results suggest that within L5 and 6, there potentially exist multiple sub-layers that receive and integrate information from different cortical and subcortical regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical observations of distinct laminar distributions.

claim: The whisker representations in POm and S2 are similarly small (~0.5 mm wide).
source: The whisker representations in POm and S2 are similarly small (~0.5 mm wide) and have known locations, lateral of VPM and S1, respectively (Carvell and Simons, 1987; Fabri and Burton, 1991a; Fabri and Burton, 1991b; Kwegyir-Afful and Keller, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple anatomical studies.

claim: POm and S2 axons arborize broadly in S1 across many columns and are similarly loosely topographic.
source: Additionally, POm and S2 axons arborize broadly in S1 across many columns and are similarly loosely topographic (Minamisawa et al., 2018; Ohno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Minamisawa et al., 2018 and Ohno et al., 2012.

claim: POm may contain multiple anterior and posterior subnuclei that preferentially innervate L5 versus L1 of barrel cortex, respectively.
source: POm may contain multiple anterior and posterior subnuclei that preferentially innervate L5 versus L1 of barrel cortex, respectively (Ohno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ohno et al., 2012.

claim: M1 cortico-callosal cells send axons which ramify in both L1 and L5/6 of barrel cortex.
source: Similarly, M1 cortico-callosal cells send axons which ramify in both L1 and L5/6 of barrel cortex, whereas corticofugal cells send more collaterals to L1 of barrel cortex (Veinante and Deschênes, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Veinante and Deschênes, 2003.

claim: M1 corticofugal cells send more collaterals to L1 of barrel cortex.
source: whereas corticofugal cells send more collaterals to L1 of barrel cortex (Veinante and Deschênes, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Veinante and Deschênes, 2003.

claim: L2/3 has been suggested to contain separate subcircuits that are active at behaviorally distinct times.
source: Additionally, L2/3 has been suggested to contain separate subcircuits that are active at behaviorally distinct times (Chen et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: POm is known to provide greater synaptic input to the most active L2/3 cells.
source: Indeed, POm is known to provide greater synaptic input to the most active L2/3 cells (Jouhanneau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jouhanneau et al., 2014.

claim: Pharmacological activation of pulvinar could enhance L2/3 neuronal responses to visual stimuli in anesthetized primates.
source: Consistent with the stronger POm effect we observed, a previous study of primary visual cortex in anesthetized primates found that pharmacological activation of pulvinar, the visual analog of POm, could enhance L2/3 neuronal responses to visual stimuli (Purushothaman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Purushothaman et al., 2012.

claim: M1 strongly activates inhibitory neurons in L2/3 of barrel cortex.
source: Also in line with the weak M1 impact here, M1 is known to strongly activate inhibitory neurons in L2/3 of barrel cortex (Kinnischtzke et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kinnischtzke et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Zagha et al., 2013.

claim: Locomotion enhances L2/3 responses in mouse V1 and suppresses primary auditory cortex.
source: Locomotion enhances L2/3 responses in mouse V1 and suppresses primary auditory cortex, but these effects may involve neuromodulation of cortical inhibitory cells as opposed to direct M1 excitatory synapses on L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Fu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2014 and Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: S2 provides only minor depolarizing inputs to L2/3 pyramidal neurons, perhaps slightly stronger than the contribution of M1.
source: We found that S2 provides only minor depolarizing inputs to L2/3 pyramidal neurons, perhaps slightly stronger than the contribution of M1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: S2 feedback had little or no effect on overall discharges of L2/3 units in S1 and may be more useful for modulating directional tuning of S1 neurons.
source: A recent study suggests that S2 feedback had little or no effect on overall discharges of L2/3 units in S1 and may be more useful for modulating directional tuning of S1 neurons (Minamisawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minamisawa et al., 2018.

claim: Coincident activation of apical and basal dendrite inputs to L5 neurons can engage large calcium spiking events in vivo, which results in supralinear integration.
source: Coincident activation of apical and basal dendrite inputs to L5 neurons can engage large calcium spiking events in vivo, which results in supralinear integration (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2012.

claim: Linear summation indicates that L4 sensory inputs and POm inputs likely innervate separate dendritic compartments of L2/3 cells.
source: Linear summation also indicates that L4 sensory inputs and POm inputs likely innervate separate dendritic compartments of L2/3 cells, whereby local depolarization by one group of synapses minimally affects the local driving force and input resistance of another dendritic compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed linear summation of inputs.

claim: L4 axons mainly innervate L2/3 basal dendrites over apical tufts.
source: This type of summation is consistent with L4 axons mainly innervating L2/3 basal dendrites over apical tufts (Lübke et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lübke et al., 2003.

claim: POm preferentially synapses on L1 apical tufts over basals.
source: and POm preferentially synapsing on L1 apical tufts over basals (Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petreanu et al., 2009.

claim: Slice studies of M1 and POm pathways using optogenetic stimulation have not revealed a major difference between M1- and POm-evoked currents.
source: However, slice studies of the individual pathways using optogenetic stimulation have not revealed a major difference between M1- and POm-evoked currents (Audette et al., 2018; Kinnischtzke et al., 2014), though these pathways have yet to be directly compared in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Audette et al., 2018 and Kinnischtzke et al., 2014.

claim: POm selectively targets 5HT3AR inhibitory cells and in vitro evokes particularly delayed inhibition in L2 relative to excitation.
source: Third, POm selectively targets 5HT3AR inhibitory cells and in vitro evokes particularly delayed inhibition in L2 relative to excitation (Audette et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Audette et al., 2018.

claim: The delayed inhibition from POm affords POm an unusually long window of integration in cortex.
source: The delayed inhibition affords POm an unusually long window of integration in cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited study on POm-evoked inhibition.

claim: POm cells have little or no recurrent connectivity with one another.
source: Since POm cells have little or no recurrent connectivity with one another (Deschênes et al., 1998; Ohno et al., 2012), the persistent firing of POm is likely due to a loop involving POm and one or more other structures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschênes et al., 1998 and Ohno et al., 2012.

claim: The persistent depolarization may be produced by reciprocally connected structures, such as POm and possibly cortical layer 5/6 and/or the thalamic reticular nucleus, perhaps with some contribution of zona incerta.
source: The persistent depolarization we observed may be produced by similarly reciprocally connected structures, such as POm and possibly cortical layer 5/6 and/or the thalamic reticular nucleus, perhaps with some contribution of zona incerta.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism of persistent depolarization.

claim: POm input can prolong suprathreshold whisker response of L5 cells on a similar timescale in isoflurane-anesthetized mice.
source: Indeed POm input can prolong suprathreshold whisker response of L5 cells on a similar timescale in isoflurane-anesthetized mice (Mease et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mease et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibitory neurons contribute to visual cortex oscillations overlapping the beta frequency range.
source: The POm input to the cortex might then act directly through projections on excitatory cells as well as indirectly through inhibitory neurons, which contribute to visual cortex oscillations overlapping the beta frequency range (Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Veit et al., 2017.

claim: Brief bursts of apical tuft input combined with broad proximal dendrite input may contribute to beta oscillation generation.
source: Recent modeling work demonstrates that brief bursts of apical tuft input combined with broad proximal dendrite input may contribute to beta oscillation generation (Sherman et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sherman et al., 2016.

claim: POm synapses are anatomically positioned to exploit the mechanism of beta oscillation generation involving apical tuft and proximal dendrite input.
source: and POm synapses are anatomically positioned to exploit precisely such a mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical knowledge of POm synapse locations and the cited modeling work.

claim: POm activity increases during active movement.
source: POm activity increases during active movement (Moore et al., 2015; Urbain et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2015 and Urbain et al., 2015.

claim: POm was recently shown to facilitate an NMDA-dependent plateau potential that can induce synaptic long-term potentiation in layer 2/3 without somatic spikes for a period on the order of ~100 ms following the stimulus.
source: First, POm was recently shown to facilitate an NMDA-dependent plateau potential that can induce synaptic long-term potentiation in layer 2/3 without somatic spikes for a period on the order of ~100 ms following the stimulus (Gambino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gambino et al., 2014.

claim: Whisker contact alone in an awake mouse does not persistently depolarize L2/3.
source: Second, whisker contact alone in an awake mouse does not persistently depolarize L2/3, but, with training on a simple tactile detection task, a prolonged secondary depolarization of unknown origin emerges.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013 (implied from context).

claim: With training on a simple tactile detection task, a prolonged secondary depolarization of unknown origin emerges in L2/3.
source: but, with training on a simple tactile detection task, a prolonged secondary depolarization of unknown origin emerges.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013 (implied from context).

claim: The late depolarization in L2/3 during behavior correlates with behavioral choices and a small increase of L2/3 firing rates.
source: This late depolarization correlates with behavioral choices and a small increase of L2/3 firing rates (albeit still sparse), and optogenetic inhibition of barrel cortex during this time period interferes with performance (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of barrel cortex during the late depolarization period interferes with performance on a tactile detection task.
source: and optogenetic inhibition of barrel cortex during this time period interferes with performance (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013.

claim: Suppressing barrel cortex activity abolishes the responses of POm neurons to whisker stimulation.
source: Suppressing barrel cortex activity abolishes the responses of POm neurons to whisker stimulation (Diamond et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diamond et al., 1992.

claim: Overall POm activity is highly elevated during wakefulness.
source: However, we found that persistent depolarizations of L2/3 via POm were absent during anesthesia. Additionally, our results and others have shown that overall POm activity is highly elevated during wakefulness (Masri et al., 2008; Urbain et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Masri et al., 2008 and Urbain et al., 2015.

claim: Elevated POm activity during wakefulness is possibly due to cholinergic regulation of zona incerta inputs to POm.
source: possibly due to cholinergic regulation of zona incerta inputs to POm (Masri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2006.

claim: POm receives connections from motor cortex and posterior parietal cortex in multiple species.
source: In addition to synapses from trigeminal brainstem and S1, POm receives connections from motor cortex and posterior parietal cortex in multiple species (Neylon and Haight, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neylon and Haight, 1983.

claim: Pulvinar lesions in non-human primates and humans impair selective attention in visual search.
source: Lesion studies in non-human primates as well as humans have demonstrated that pulvinar is important for selective attention in visual search (Bender and Butter, 1987; Ungerleider and Christensen, 1979; Ward et al., 2002; Wilke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bender and Butter, 1987; Ungerleider and Christensen, 1979; Ward et al., 2002; Wilke et al., 2010.

claim: Responses of pulvinar neurons are stronger when stimuli are presented within an attended region of visual space.
source: Behavioral studies further demonstrated that responses of pulvinar neurons are stronger when stimuli are presented within an attended region of visual space (Petersen et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petersen et al., 1985.

claim: Pulvinar neurons corresponding to the attended location fire tonically at elevated levels prior to stimulus presentation.
source: Pulvinar neurons corresponding to the attended location also fire tonically at elevated levels prior to stimulus presentation, suggesting that pulvinar may be involved in allocating spatial attention and/or maintaining working memory (Saalmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saalmann et al., 2012.

claim: Activity in pulvinar and visual cortical areas is highly coherent in beta-range frequencies.
source: Intriguingly, activity in pulvinar and visual cortical areas is highly coherent in beta-range frequencies (Saalmann et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saalmann et al., 2012.

claim: POm lesions do not affect an animal's ability to detect passive deflection of a single whisker.
source: One behavioral study concluded that POm lesions do not affect an animal's ability to detect passive deflection of a single whisker (Narumi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Narumi et al., 2007.

claim: POm may be primarily engaged during active sensing with multiple whiskers given its large receptive fields and tight reciprocal connections with M1 and S1.
source: However, POm may be primarily engaged during active sensing with multiple whiskers given its large receptive fields and tight reciprocal connections with M1 and S1 (Diamond et al., 1992; Groh et al., 2014; Groh et al., 2008; Miyashita et al., 1994; Trageser and Keller, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diamond et al., 1992; Groh et al., 2014; Groh et al., 2008; Miyashita et al., 1994; Trageser and Keller, 2004.

claim: POm sensory responses can be significantly boosted by the presence of neuromodulators.
source: Physiological studies have demonstrated that POm sensory responses can be significantly boosted by the presence of neuromodulators (Masri et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2006.

claim: Subsets of POm neurons are highly responsive to noxious stimuli.
source: Additionally, subsets of POm neurons are highly responsive to noxious stimuli (Masri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2009.

claim: POm may respond to any stimuli of high behavioral salience rather than selectively representing pain.
source: However, rather than selectively representing pain, POm may respond to any stimuli of high behavioral salience.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited findings.

claim: Secondary sensory nuclei in thalamus may enable encoding of high-order contextual information during behavior via the long-lasting input they provide to L2/3.
source: Secondary sensory nuclei in thalamus may enable encoding of such high-order contextual information during behavior (Saalmann et al., 2012) via the long-lasting input they provide to L2/3.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Long-lasting POm input may render L2/3 sensitive to conjunctions of sensory and contextual inputs.
source: This may render L2/3 sensitive to conjunctions of sensory and contextual inputs and provide an eligibility trace enabling plasticity over behavioral timescales.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: Long-lasting POm input may provide an eligibility trace enabling plasticity over behavioral timescales.
source: This may render L2/3 sensitive to conjunctions of sensory and contextual inputs and provide an eligibility trace enabling plasticity over behavioral timescales.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the functional implications of the findings.
